questions.q: What are the two main character traits of the conductor highlighted in the story?
questions.a: The two main traits are kindness and humour. A wrong answer (e.g., “strictness and anger”) shows the student has not distinguished the conductor from other adult figures like the bus driver or the elderly woman who scolds Valli.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the conductor’s humour differs from the humour in Valli’s internal thoughts.
questions.a: The conductor’s humour is external, spoken aloud to put Valli at ease (e.g., calling her ‘madam’ playfully), while Valli’s humour is internal, ironic, and often critical of adults. A wrong answer that conflates the two indicates the student cannot separate narrative voice from character dialogue.

questions.q: Find one example of the conductor’s kindness that is NOT the offer of a cold drink. Quote the exact words or describe the action precisely.
questions.a: Example: When the conductor says, “Never mind, I’ll get you a seat,” and physically arranges a seat for her. A wrong answer that repeats the cold‑drink offer shows the student relies on a single memorable detail instead of scanning the whole text.

questions.q: Compare the conductor’s attitude toward Valli with the elderly woman’s attitude. What does this contrast reveal about the story’s view of adulthood?
questions.a: The conductor treats Valli with respect and playfulness; the elderly woman treats her with condescension and intrusion. The contrast shows adulthood is not monolithic – some adults nurture a child’s independence while others stifle it. A wrong answer that merely lists behaviours without interpreting the thematic implication reveals a surface‑level reading.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the conductor’s humour ever crosses the line into mockery. Support your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: No, his humour is always affectionate – e.g., “Oh, please don’t be angry with me, madam” – and Valli never feels mocked; she enjoys the banter. A wrong answer that claims he mocks her ignores Valli’s own reactions (she smiles, replies confidently) and misreads the tone.

questions.q: Write a short diary entry (4‑5 lines) from the conductor’s perspective describing his encounter with Valli, incorporating both his kindness and his humour.
questions.a: A good entry will use first‑person voice, mention calling her ‘madam’, offering a drink, and a light‑hearted remark like “You’re a bold passenger, madam.” A poor entry will either omit one trait or write in third person, showing the student cannot adopt the character’s perspective.
